entries.original_title: Perceived entitativity, stereotype formation, and the interchangeability of group members
entries.original_authors: Crawford, M.; Sherman, S.; Hamilton, D.
entries.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
entries.description: When a group is perceived as large and diverse, people recognize that one individual's behavior is not representative of all group members and resist generalizing evaluations to another group member.
entries.citation_sentence: We predicted that people would explicitly refrain from using the information about the original group members in making immediate judgments of the new group members; this finding would replicate demonstrations that people can recognize that one individual's behavior is not representative of all group members if their group is large and diverse [5][17].
entries.notes: The paper cites the original using numbered references rather than author-year citations. The replication found that explicit generalization was substantially reduced for new group members, although not entirely absent.

entries.original_title: Target entitativity: Implications for information processing about individual and group targets
entries.original_authors: McConnell, A.; Sherman, S.; Hamilton, D.
entries.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
entries.description: People can recognize that one individual's behavior is not representative of all members of a large and diverse group and therefore resist transferring evaluations from one group member to another.
entries.citation_sentence: We predicted that people would explicitly refrain from using the information about the original group members in making immediate judgments of the new group members; this finding would replicate demonstrations that people can recognize that one individual's behavior is not representative of all group members if their group is large and diverse [5][17].
entries.notes: The paper cites the original using numbered references rather than author-year citations. The replication found that explicit generalization was substantially reduced for new group members, although not entirely absent.
